questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: The number of permutations of the letters of the word INSTITUTION are.......
questions.solution:
The word INSTITUTION has $11$ letters.

The frequencies of the letters are:
I appears $3$ times.
N appears $2$ times.
T appears $3$ times.
S, U, O appear $1$ time each.

The total number of permutations is given by $\dfrac{11!}{3! \times 2! \times 3!}$.

$\dfrac{11!}{3! \times 2! \times 3!} = \dfrac{39916800}{6 \times 2 \times 6} = \dfrac{39916800}{72} = 554400$

Answer: $554400$

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: Four men and three women are to be arranged at a round table. The number of arrangements in which no two women are together is....
questions.solution:
First, arrange the $4$ men around the circular table. The number of ways to do this is $(4 - 1)! = 3!$.

When the $4$ men are seated, they create $4$ gaps between them.

To ensure that no two women sit together, the $3$ women must be placed in these $4$ gaps.

The number of ways to choose $3$ gaps out of $4$ and arrange the $3$ women in them is ^{4}P_{3} = 4 \times 3 \times 2 = 4!$.

Therefore, the total number of arrangements is 3! \times 4!$.

Answer: $3! \times 4!$

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: In a test, there are 7 questions of the type 'True or False'. No student got all the answers correct. If the sequence of answers for every student is unique, then the maximum number of students who appeared for the test is $\ldots$
questions.solution:
Total number of questions = $7$

Each question can be answered in $2$ ways (True or False).

Total number of possible answer sequences = $2^7 = 128$

Since no student got all the answers correct, the sequence corresponding to all correct answers is excluded.

Number of available sequences = $128 - 1 = 127$

Since every student's sequence of answers is unique, the maximum number of students is equal to the number of available sequences.

Maximum number of students = $127$

Answer: $127$

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: 11 players of the Indian cricket team are sitting at a circular table. The number of ways they can sit so that two players, the wicket keeper and the captain never sit together is ___
questions.solution:
Total number of players is $11$.

Total number of ways to arrange $11$ players around a circular table is $(11 - 1)! = 10!$.

To find the number of ways where the wicket keeper and the captain sit together, consider them as a single unit.

The number of units to arrange is $9$ remaining players plus $1$ unit, which equals $10$ units.

The number of ways to arrange these $10$ units around a circular table is $(10 - 1)! = 9!$.

The wicket keeper and the captain can interchange their positions within the unit in $2! = 2$ ways.

The number of ways they sit together is $2 \times 9!$.

The number of ways they never sit together is the total number of ways minus the number of ways they sit together.

Required number of ways is $10! - 2 \times 9! = 10 \times 9! - 2 \times 9! = 8 \times 9!$.

Answer: $8 \times 9!$

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: In a test, there are 5 questions of the 'true or false' type. No student has got all the answers correct and the sequence of answers for every student is unique. The maximum number of students who could have appeared for the test is....
questions.solution:
The test has $5$ questions, and each question has $2$ possible answers (True or False).

The total number of possible sequences of answers is $2^5 = 32$.

Out of these $32$ sequences, exactly $1$ sequence corresponds to all answers being correct.

Since no student has got all the answers correct, this specific sequence cannot be chosen by any student.

The number of available sequences of answers is $32 - 1 = 31$.

Since the sequence of answers for every student is unique, the maximum number of students who could have appeared for the test is equal to the maximum number of available unique sequences, which is $31$.

Answer: $31$

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: The number of arrangements of the letters in the word SOLAPUR, so that consonants and vowels are placed alternately is
questions.solution:
The word SOLAPUR consists of 7 letters.

The vowels are O, A, U (3 vowels).

The consonants are S, L, P, R (4 consonants).

Since consonants and vowels must be placed alternately and there are 4 consonants and 3 vowels, the arrangement must start and end with a consonant. The only possible pattern is C V C V C V C, where C represents a consonant and V represents a vowel.

The 4 consonants can be arranged in the 4 alternate positions in $4!$ ways.

The 3 vowels can be arranged in the 3 remaining alternate positions in $3!$ ways.

Total number of arrangements is $4! \times 3!$.

$24 \times 6 = 144$

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: The number of 4-letter words formed from the English alphabet such that there are exactly 2 vowels and 2 consonants and no vowel is repeated, but consonants may be repeated is:
questions.solution:
The 4-letter word requires exactly 2 vowels and 2 consonants.

The number of ways to choose 2 positions out of 4 for the vowels is ^{4}C_{2}$.

Since no vowel is repeated, the number of ways to choose and arrange 2 distinct vowels from the 5 available vowels in the chosen positions is ^{5}P_{2}$.

The remaining 2 positions must be filled with consonants. Since there are 21 consonants and repetition is allowed, each position can be filled in 21 ways. The number of ways to fill the consonant positions is $21 \times 21 = (21)^2$.

The total number of 4-letter words formed is ^{4}C_{2} \times ^{5}P_{2} \times (21)^2$.

Answer: ${}^{4}C_2 \times {}^{5}P_2 \times (21)^2

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: The number of arrangements of the numbers strictly between 10 and 1000 formed with the digits 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 without repetition is
questions.solution:
The numbers between $10$ and $1000$ consist of $2$-digit and $3$-digit numbers, strictly greater than $10$.

Available digits: $0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6$ (a total of $7$ digits).

For $2$-digit numbers:
The tens place can be filled in $6$ ways (excluding $0$).
The units place can be filled in $6$ ways (any of the remaining $6$ digits, including $0$).
Total $2$-digit numbers formed = $6 \times 6 = 36$.
Since the numbers must be strictly between $10$ and $1000$, the number $10$ itself must be excluded.
Valid $2$-digit numbers = $36 - 1 = 35$.

For $3$-digit numbers:
The hundreds place can be filled in $6$ ways (excluding $0$).
The tens place can be filled in $6$ ways.
The units place can be filled in $5$ ways.
Total $3$-digit numbers formed = $6 \times 6 \times 5 = 180$.

Total valid numbers = $35 + 180 = 215$.

Answer: $215$

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: A bag contains 23 balls, of which 7 are identical. The number of ways of selecting 12 balls from the bag is....
questions.solution:
Total number of balls = $23$
Number of identical balls = $7$
Number of distinct balls = $23 - 7 = 16$

We need to select $12$ balls. Let the number of identical balls selected be $k$, where $0 \le k \le 7$.
The remaining $12 - k$ balls must be selected from the $16$ distinct balls. The number of ways to do this is $\binom{16}{12-k}$.

The total number of ways to select $12$ balls is the sum of these possibilities for $k = 0$ to $7$:
$S = \sum_{k=0}^{7} \binom{16}{12-k}$
$S = \binom{16}{12} + \binom{16}{11} + \binom{16}{10} + \binom{16}{9} + \binom{16}{8} + \binom{16}{7} + \binom{16}{6} + \binom{16}{5}$

Using the property $\binom{n}{r} = \binom{n}{n-r}$, we can rewrite the first four terms:
$\binom{16}{12} = \binom{16}{4}$
$\binom{16}{11} = \binom{16}{5}$
$\binom{16}{10} = \binom{16}{6}$
$\binom{16}{9} = \binom{16}{7}$

Substituting these back into the sum:
$S = \binom{16}{4} + \binom{16}{5} + \binom{16}{6} + \binom{16}{7} + \binom{16}{8} + \binom{16}{7} + \binom{16}{6} + \binom{16}{5}$

Rearranging and grouping the terms:
$S = (\binom{16}{4} + \binom{16}{5}) + (\binom{16}{5} + \binom{16}{6}) + (\binom{16}{6} + \binom{16}{7}) + (\binom{16}{7} + \binom{16}{8})$

Using Pascal's identity $\binom{n}{r} + \binom{n}{r-1} = \binom{n+1}{r}$:
$S = \binom{17}{5} + \binom{17}{6} + \binom{17}{7} + \binom{17}{8}$

Grouping again:
$S = (\binom{17}{5} + \binom{17}{6}) + (\binom{17}{7} + \binom{17}{8})$
$S = \binom{18}{6} + \binom{18}{8}$

Answer: ${}^{18}C_6 + {}^{18}C_8$

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: If 6 boys and 3 girls are to be seated in a row for a photograph, then the probability that the end seats are occupied by the girls and no two girls are side by side is
questions.solution:
Total number of arrangements of $6$ boys and $3$ girls in a row is $9!$.

For the end seats to be occupied by girls, we can select and arrange $2$ girls out of $3$ in ^{3}P_{2} = 6$ ways.

The remaining 1$ girl and $6$ boys are to be seated in the remaining $7$ middle seats. To ensure no two girls are side by side, the remaining $1$ girl cannot sit in the seats adjacent to the ends (i.e., the 2nd and 8th seats).

Thus, the remaining girl can sit in any of the $5$ available middle seats (3rd, 4th, 5th, 6th, or 7th).

The $6$ boys can then be arranged in the remaining $6$ seats in $6!$ ways.

Total number of favorable arrangements is $6 \times 5 \times 6! = 30 \times 6!$.

The required probability is $\dfrac{30 \times 6!}{9!} = \dfrac{30}{9 \times 8 \times 7} = \dfrac{5}{84}$.

Answer: $\dfrac{5}{84}$

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: The number of five-digit numbers formed using the digits $2, 3, 5, 7, 9$ without repetition and which are greater than $24000$ are
questions.solution:
The total number of five-digit numbers that can be formed using the digits $2, 3, 5, 7, 9$ without repetition is $5! = 120$.

For a number to be less than $24000$, it must start with $2$ and the second digit must be less than $4$.

From the given digits, the only possible second digit less than $4$ is $3$. Thus, the numbers less than $24000$ must be of the form $23XXX$.

The remaining three positions can be filled by the remaining three digits (5, 7, 9$) in 3! = 6$ ways.

Therefore, the number of five-digit numbers greater than $24000$ is $120 - 6 = 114$.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: The number of cubic equations that can be formed with the coefficients 0, 3, 2, 4, 5, 6 when repetition of coefficients is allowed, is....
questions.solution:
A cubic equation is of the form $ax^3 + bx^2 + cx + d = 0$, where $a \neq 0$.

The given set of coefficients is $\{0, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6\}$, which contains 6 elements.

Since $a \neq 0$, the coefficient $a$ can be chosen in 5 ways (any number from the set except 0).

The coefficients $b, c,$ and $d$ can each be chosen in 6 ways, as repetition of coefficients is allowed.

Total number of cubic equations $= 5 \times 6 \times 6 \times 6 = 1080$.

Answer: $1080$

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: The number of ways that 8 beads of different colours can be strung to form a necklace is
questions.solution:
The number of ways to arrange $n$ distinct objects in a circle is $(n-1)!$.

For a necklace, clockwise and counter-clockwise arrangements are considered identical because it can be flipped over.

Therefore, the number of ways to string $n$ different beads into a necklace is $\dfrac{(n-1)!}{2}$.

Given $n = 8$, the number of ways is $\dfrac{(8-1)!}{2} = \dfrac{7!}{2}$.

Since $7! = 5040$, the number of ways is $\dfrac{5040}{2} = 2520$.

Answer: $2520$

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: There are $5$ boys and $3$ girls seated in a row for a photograph. The number of ways in which a photograph can be taken if the girls occupy only odd places is...
questions.solution:
Total number of persons is $5 + 3 = 8$.

The seats are numbered $1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8$.

The odd places are $1, 3, 5, 7$. There are $4$ odd places.

The $3$ girls can be seated in these $4$ odd places in ^{4}P_{3}$ ways.

^{4}P_{3} = 24$

After seating the girls, there are $5$ seats remaining (1$ odd and 4$ even places).

The $5$ boys can be seated in the remaining $5$ places in $5!$ ways.

$5! = 120$

Total number of ways $= 24 \times 120 = 2880$.

Answer: $2880$

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: Let $m$ denotes the number of ways in which 5 boys and 5 girls can be arranged in a line alternately and n denotes the number of ways in which 5 boys and 5 girls can be arranged in a circle so that no two boys are together. If $m=k n$, then the value of $k$ is
questions.solution:
There are two alternating gender patterns in a linear arrangement: $BGBGBGBGBG$ and $GBGBGBGBGB$.

Each pattern has $5!$ arrangements for boys and $5!$ for girls, contributing $5! \times 5!$ ways each.

Thus, $m = 2 \times (5! \times 5!) = 2 \times (120 \times 120) = 28800$.

For circular arrangements with no adjacent boys, first arrange the girls in $(5-1)! = 4! = 24$ ways around the circle.

This creates 5 distinct gaps between girls, where the 5 boys can be arranged in $5! = 120$ ways.

Hence, $n = 4! \times 5! = 24 \times 120 = 2880$.

Given $m = k n$, we compute $k = \frac{m}{n} = \frac{28800}{2880} = 10$.

The value is therefore $\boxed{\text{D}}$.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: The number of ways in which 6 boys and 4 girls can be seated around a round table such that 2 special boys and a special girl never sit together is
questions.solution:
Circular arrangements with restrictions are computed using complementary counting. The total arrangements of 10 distinct people around a circular table is $(10-1)! = 9!$.

To count arrangements where two special boys and one special girl always sit together, treat them as a single block. Within this block, they can be arranged in $3!$ ways. With the block considered as one entity, there remain 7 people, giving $(8-1)! = 7!$ circular arrangements. The number of restricted arrangements is therefore $3! \times 7!$.

The number of valid arrangements where the specified individuals never sit together is:

$9! - (3! \times 7!) = 362880 - 30240 = 332640$

The final answer is $\boxed{332640}$.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: The number of ways in which a team of 11 players can be formed out of 25 players, if 6 out of them are always to be included and 5 of them are always to be excluded, is
questions.solution:
Given 25 players, with 6 players always included and 5 players always excluded, to form an 11-player team, we first exclude the 5 players who cannot participate and note that 6 players are fixed. The remaining 5 positions must be chosen from the effective pool of $25 - 6 - 5 = 14$ players.

The selection is a combination: $\binom{14}{5} = \frac{14 \times 13 \times 12 \times 11 \times 10}{5 \times 4 \times 3 \times 2 \times 1} = 2002$.

Final answer: $2002$.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: There are 11 points in a plane of which 5 points are collinear. Then the total number of distinct quadrilaterals with vertices at these points is
questions.solution:
A quadrilateral requires selecting four points with no three collinear. Given 11 total points including five collinear, the valid selections are determined by excluding invalid cases.

The total ways to choose any four points is $C(11,4)=330$.

Invalid combinations occur if all four points are collinear, which gives $C(5,4)=5$ cases, or if three are collinear and one is not, yielding $C(5,3)\times C(6,1)=60$ cases.

Subtracting these from the total gives $330-5-60=265$ distinct quadrilaterals.

Answer: $\boxed{265}$

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: A family consisting of a mother, father and their 8 children ( 4 boys and 4 girls) are to be seated at a round table in a party. How many ways can this be done if the mother and father sit together and the males and females alternate?
questions.solution:
Given a family of 10 people—mother, father, 4 boys, and 4 girls—arranged around a round table with alternating genders and the mother and father seated together.

The table alternates between 5 male and 5 female positions. Fix the mother in a female seat to account for circular symmetry. The father must occupy an adjacent male seat to satisfy the togetherness condition. The arrangement of the remaining 4 girls and 4 boys in the vacant female and male seats is $4! \times 4! = 576$.

The final count is $576$.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: If four digit numbers are formed by using the digits $1,2,3,4,5,6,7$ without repetition, then out of these numbers, the numbers exactly divisible by 25 are
questions.solution:
For a four-digit number formed from the digits $\{1,2,3,4,5,6,7\}$ to be divisible by 25, its last two digits must form a number divisible by 25.

The possible two-digit endings are $25$ and $75$, as $00$ and $50$ are not feasible without the digit $0$.

Case ending in 25: The digits 2 and 5 are used, leaving $\{1,3,4,6,7\}$ for the first two positions. There are $5 \times 4 = 20$ arrangements.

Case ending in 75: The digits 7 and 5 are used, leaving $\{1,2,3,4,6\}$ for the first two positions. There are $5 \times 4 = 20$ arrangements.

Total numbers: $20 + 20 = 40$.

The number of valid four-digit numbers divisible by 25 is $\boxed{40}$.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: 21 friends were invited for a party. Two round tables can accommodate 12 and 9 friends each. The number of ways of the seating arrangements of friends is.....
questions.solution:
The arrangement involves partitioning the 21 friends into groups of 12 and 9, then arranging them at round tables where only relative order matters.

The number of ways to select 12 friends for the first table is $\binom{21}{12} = \frac{21!}{12!9!}$, with the remaining 9 assigned to the second table.

For each table with $n$ persons, circular permutations yield $(n-1)!$ distinct arrangements: $11!$ for the first table and $8!$ for the second.

Multiplying the selection and arrangement counts gives $\frac{21!}{12!9!} \cdot 11! \cdot 8!$.

Simplifying, since $12! = 12 \times 11!$ and $9! = 9 \times 8!$, we substitute to get $\frac{21!}{(12 \cdot 11!)(9 \cdot 8!)} \cdot 11! \cdot 8! = \frac{21!}{12 \cdot 9} = \frac{21!}{108}$.

Reducing the fraction $\frac{21!}{108}$ by the greatest common divisor (12) gives $\frac{35 \cdot 19!}{9}$, matching option C.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
Applying the symmetry property ${}^N C_R = {}^N C_{N-R}$, we rewrite:

$\binom{n+4}{n+1} = {}^{n+4} C_3$
${}^{n+3} C_n = {}^{n+3} C_3$

The original equation becomes:

${}^{n+4} C_3 - {}^{n+3} C_3 = 15(n+2)$

Using the identity ${}^N C_R - {}^{N-1} C_R = \binom{N-1}{R-1}$ with $N = n+4$ and $R = 3$:

${}^{n+4} C_3 - {}^{n+3} C_3 = {}^{n+3} C_2$

Thus, the equation simplifies to:

${}^{n+3} C_2 = 15(n+2)$

Expanding the combination:

${}^{n+3} C_2 = \frac{(n+3)(n+2)}{2}$

Substituting back:

$\frac{(n+3)(n+2)}{2} = 15(n+2)$

Since $n \ge 0$ for valid combinations, we can divide both sides by $(n+2)$:

$\frac{n+3}{2} = 15$

Solving yields $n = 27$.

Final answer: $\boxed{D}$

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: The greatest possible number of points of intersection of 8 distinct straight lines and 4 distinct circles is
questions.solution:
To determine the maximum number of intersection points among 8 distinct straight lines and 4 distinct circles, consider all possible pairwise intersections.

Intersections between lines: Each pair of lines intersects at most once, yielding $\binom{8}{2} = 28$ points.

Intersections between circles: Each pair of circles intersects at most twice, giving $2 \times \binom{4}{2} = 12$ points.

Intersections between lines and circles: Each line and circle intersect at most twice, contributing $2 \times 8 \times 4 = 64$ points.

Summing these independent cases, the total maximum is $28 + 12 + 64 = 104$.

$\boxed{104}$

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: The probability that in a random arrangement of the letters of the word 'UNIVERSITY' , the two 'I' s do not come together is
questions.solution:
Probability that the two 'I's do not come together in an arrangement of 'UNIVERSITY'

The word 'UNIVERSITY' contains 10 letters with 'I' appearing twice; all other letters are unique. The total number of distinct arrangements is given by $\frac{10!}{2!} = 1,814,400$.

Treating the two 'I's as a single block yields 9 distinct units. The number of arrangements where the 'I's are together is $9! = 362,880$.

The complementary probability approach gives:
$P(\text{'I's not together}) = 1 - P(\text{'I's together}) = 1 - \frac{9!}{\frac{10!}{2!}} = 1 - \frac{2}{10} = \frac{4}{5}$.

The probability is therefore $\frac{4}{5}$.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: 4 red balls and 5 green balls are selected from n balls. If the sum of both the selections is greater then ${ }^{n+1} C_4$ then the value of $n$ is equal to
questions.solution:
The problem requires finding for which n the sum of selecting 4 red balls and 5 green balls from n balls each exceeds C(n+1, 4). The inequality is C(n, 4) + C(n, 5) > C(n+1, 4).

Applying Pascal's identity, C(n, 4) + C(n, 5) = C(n+1, 5), so the inequality becomes C(n+1, 5) > C(n+1, 4).

Expressing both sides with factorials, $\frac{(n+1)!}{5!(n-4)!} > \frac{(n+1)!}{4!(n-3)!}$, and simplifying leads to $n - 3 > 5$, so $n > 8$.

Given the options, the correct choice is A.
Final answer: $\boxed{A}$

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: A regular polygon has 20 sides. The number of triangles that can be drawn by using the vertices but not using the sides are
questions.solution:
The number of triangles formed from vertices of a regular 20-gon without using polygon sides equals the count of triangles that share no sides with the polygon.

The total number of triangles is given by $C(20,3) = \frac{20 \times 19 \times 18}{3 \times 2 \times 1} = 1140$.

Triangles sharing exactly two sides correspond to three consecutive vertices, yielding $20$ such triangles.
Triangles sharing exactly one side are formed by selecting one side (20$ choices) and a non-adjacent third vertex (20 - 4 = 16$ choices), giving $20 \times 16 = 320$ triangles.

The count of triangles sharing no sides is then $1140 - (20 + 320) = 800$.

Final answer: $\boxed{800}$

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: Total number of 3-digit numbers, whose g.c.d with 36 is 2 , is
questions.solution:
Given that $\gcd(N, 36) = 2$, and $36 = 2^2 \cdot 3^2$, we require $N$ to be even but not divisible by $4$ or $3$. Since $100 \le N \le 999$, write $N = 2k$ with $k$ an integer satisfying $50 \le k \le 499$. Further, $k$ must be odd to ensure $N$ is not divisible by $4$.

The count of odd integers from $50$ to $499$ is $\frac{499 - 51}{2} + 1 = 225$.

To ensure $\gcd(N, 36) = 2$, $k$ must not be a multiple of $3$. The number of odd multiples of $3$ in this range is $\frac{165 - 17}{2} + 1 = 75$.

Hence, the number of valid $k$ is $225 - 75 = 150$, each giving a unique $N = 2k$.

Final answer: $\boxed{150}$

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: The number of ways, in which 6 boys and 5 girls can sit at a round table, if no two girls are to sit together, is
questions.solution:
With 6 distinguishable boys, the number of distinct circular arrangements is $(6-1)! = 5! = 120$.

These boys create 6 distinct spaces for seating the 5 distinguishable girls, ensuring no two girls are adjacent. The number of ways to choose 5 of the 6 spaces is $C(6,5) = 6$. The number of ways to arrange the 5 girls among the chosen spaces is $5! = 120$.

The total number of seating arrangements is the product: $5! \times C(6,5) \times 5! = 120 \times 6 \times 120 = 86400$.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: A five digit number divisible by 3 is to be formed using the digits $0,1,2,3,4,5$ without repetition, then the total number of ways this can be done is
questions.solution:
We know that a five digit number is divisible by 3 , if and only if sum of its digits $(=15)$ is divisible by 3. Therefore, we should not use 0 and 3 in a same number while forming the five digit numbers.
Now,
i. In case we do not use 0 , the five digit number can be formed (using digits $1,2,3,4,5$ ) in ${ }^5 \mathrm{P}_5=120$ ways.
ii. In case we do not use 3, the five digit number can be formed (using digits $0,1,2,4,5$ ) in ${ }^5 \mathrm{P}_5-{ }^4 \mathrm{P}_4=5!-4!=120-24=96$ ways
$\therefore \quad$ The total number of such 5 digit number $=120+96=216$

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: Eight chairs are numbered 1 to 8. Two women and three men wish to occupy one chair each. First the women choose chairs from amongst the chairs marked 1 to 4 , and then the men select the chairs from amongst the remaining. The number of possible arrangements is
questions.solution:
Two women can be made to sit on chairs marked 1 to 4 in ${ }^4 P_2$ ways and then three men can be seated in 6 available seats in ${ }^6 \mathrm{P}_3$ ways.
$\therefore \quad$ number of possible arrangements is ${ }^4 \mathrm{P}_2 \times{ }^6 \mathrm{P}_3$.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: There are 3 sections in a question paper and each section contains 5 questions. A candidate has to answer a total of 5 questions, choosing at least one question from each section. Then the number of ways, in which the candidate can choose the questions, is
questions.solution:
Total number of $ways
\begin{aligned}
&={ }^5 \mathrm{C}_1 \times{ }^5 \mathrm{C}_1 \times{ }^5 \mathrm{C}_3+{ }^5 \mathrm{C}_1 \times{ }^5 \mathrm{C}_2 \times{ }^5 \mathrm{C}_2 \\
&+{ }^5 \mathrm{C}_1 \times{ }^5 \mathrm{C}_3 \times{ }^5 \mathrm{C}_1+{ }^5 \mathrm{C}_2 \times{ }^5 \mathrm{C}_1 \times{ }^5 \mathrm{C}_2 \\
&+{ }^5 \mathrm{C}_2 \times{ }^5 \mathrm{C}_2 \times{ }^5 \mathrm{C}_1+{ }^5 \mathrm{C}_3 \times{ }^5 \mathrm{C}_1 \times{ }^5 \mathrm{C}_1 \\
&=5 \times 5 \times 10+5 \times 10 \times 10+5 \times 10 \times 5 \\
& \quad+10 \times 5 \times 10+10 \times 10 \times 5+10 \times 5 \times 5 \\
&= 250+500+250+500+500+250 \\
&= 2250
\end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: The number of arrangements, of the letters of the word MANAMA in which two M's do not appear adjacent, is
questions.solution:
There are 6 letters.
M repeats 2 times,
A repeats 3 times.
We first arrange all letters except $2 \mathrmM^{\prime} \mathrm{s}$ in $\frac{4!}{3!}=4$ ways
These 4 letters create 5 gaps, where we can arrange $2 \mathrmM^{\prime} \mathrm{s}$ in $\frac{{ }^5 \mathrm{p}_2}{2!}=10$ ways
$\therefore \quad$ Required number of arrangements $=4 \times 10=40$

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: $\qquad$ numbers greater than a million can be formed with the digits $2,3,0,3,4,2,3$.
questions.solution:
All seven-digit numbers formed with the given digits are greater than a million.
Note that the digit at millions place cannot be 0 .
$\therefore \quad$ It can be any one of the digits $2,3,4$.
Case I :
Digit at millions place is ' 2 '.
Remaining 6 digits can be arranged in $\frac{6!}{3!}=120$ ways.
Case II :
Digit at millions place is ' 3 '.

$\therefore \quad$ Required number of ways $=3 \times 5 \times 2=30$.
